draft.title: Inverse functions
card: A function is one-to-one if each y-value comes from only one x-value. A horizontal line cuts its graph at most once. Only a one-to-one function has an inverse function.
The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f. Its domain is the range of f, and its range is the domain of f. The graphs are reflections of each other in the line y = x.
To find f⁻¹, swap x and y, then solve for y. Example: f(x) = 2x + 3. Swap: x = 2y + 3. Solve: y = (x − 3)/2. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.
y = x² is not one-to-one, as x = 2 and x = −2 both give 4. Restrict the domain, such as x ≥ 0, and it becomes one-to-one. Then the inverse is f⁻¹(x) = √x.
draft.remember: Swap x and y to find the inverse. Its domain is the range of f.

a.q: f(x) = 3x − 6 is a one-to-one function. What is f⁻¹(x)?
a.why: Swap to get x = 3y − 6. Add 6 to get x + 6 = 3y, so y = (x + 6)/3. (x − 6)/3 is tempting, but it subtracts 6 when the inverse must undo the subtraction by adding 6.
a.clue: Swap x and y, then solve for y.

b.q: g(x) = (x − 2)², with domain x ≥ 2. What are the domain and rule of g⁻¹?
b.why: The range of g is y ≥ 0, so the domain of g⁻¹ is x ≥ 0. Swap: x = (y − 2)², so y − 2 = √x since y ≥ 2, and y = √x + 2. Using the domain of g as the domain of g⁻¹ is the tempting mistake.
b.clue: The domain of the inverse is the range of g, not the domain of g.

final.title: Inverse functions
card: A function is one-to-one if each y-value comes from only one x-value. A horizontal line cuts its graph at most once. Only a one-to-one function has an inverse function.
The inverse \(f^{-1}\) undoes \(f\). Its domain is the range of \(f\), and its range is the domain of \(f\). The graphs are reflections of each other in the line \(y = x\).
To find \(f^{-1}\), swap \(x\) and \(y\), then solve for \(y\). Example: \(f(x) = 2x + 3\). Swap: \(x = 2y + 3\). Solve: \(y = \frac{x - 3}{2}\). So \(f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x - 3}{2}\).
\(y = x^{2}\) is not one-to-one, as \(x = 2\) and \(x = -2\) both give 4. Restrict the domain, such as \(x \ge 0\), and it becomes one-to-one. Then the inverse is \(f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x}\).

4.alt: The graph of \(y = x^{2}\) for \(x \ge 0\) and its inverse \(y = \sqrt{x}\), reflections of each other in the dotted line \(y = x\). The point \((2, 4)\) on \(y = x^{2}\) matches \((4, 2)\) on \(y = \sqrt{x}\). Both start at the origin.

final.remember: Swap \(x\) and \(y\) to find the inverse. Its domain is the range of \(f\).

a.q: \(f(x) = 3x - 6\) is a one-to-one function. What is \(f^{-1}(x)\)?
a.why: Swap to get \(x = 3y - 6\). Add 6 to get \(x + 6 = 3y\), so \(y = \frac{x + 6}{3}\). \(\frac{x - 6}{3}\) is tempting, but it subtracts 6 when the inverse must undo the subtraction by adding 6.

b.q: \(g(x) = (x - 2)^{2}\), with domain \(x \ge 2\). What are the domain and rule of \(g^{-1}\)?
b.why: The range of \(g\) is \(y \ge 0\), so the domain of \(g^{-1}\) is \(x \ge 0\). Swap: \(x = (y - 2)^{2}\), so \(y - 2 = \sqrt{x}\) since \(y \ge 2\), and \(y = \sqrt{x} + 2\). Using the domain of \(g\) as the domain of \(g^{-1}\) is the tempting mistake.
b.clue: The domain of the inverse is the range of \(g\), not the domain of \(g\).
